title: A Pair of Important Lessons from the Demise of G3
author: Tim Challies
summary: Challies uses the collapse of a conference ministry to argue that removing a disgraced leader is necessary but almost never sufficient. He recounts raising a concern after the founder resigned for anonymously slandering other leaders, namely that the organisation had moved fast on the man and slowly on itself, and then notes that a year later all four elders of the associated church were caught circulating anonymous material about another pastor. The repetition is his evidence: the second offence involved the same secrecy, meddling and refusal to go to a brother directly as the first. From this he draws two lessons. The first is that a founder's weaknesses are embedded in the organisation as surely as his strengths, so a wise leader builds policy, limits and complementary hires against his own flaws, and a successor organisation must examine whether those flaws are woven into its fabric. The second is that condemning a sin in someone else is itself a dangerous moment, since we rarely hold ourselves to the standard we apply to others, a danger he admits he feels in writing the article. The piece is candid that there is only one kind of leader available, the flawed kind, and that the wise ones go looking for their flaws and invite others to do the same.
points: Argues the failure was sequential rather than coincidental: right action against the founder substituted for self-examination of the culture he built.
Treats the near-identical pattern of the second scandal as evidence that the sin was structural, not personal to one man.
Recommends concrete countermeasures for a leader's known weaknesses, including policy limits and hiring for the strengths he lacks.
Names the act of judging another's sin as a moment of specific danger, and applies the warning to his own writing of the piece.
Distinguishes a flawed leader from a disqualified one, locating the difference in whether he actively seeks out his flaws and invites scrutiny.
quotes: Just as a founder’s strengths will be embedded in the organization he creates, so will his weaknesses.
Though the two sins happened a year apart, they were of a similar kind, involving secrecy, meddling, accusation, and a failure to go directly to a brother
Thus, a wise leader tries to gain an awareness of his weaknesses and in some way to oppose or mitigate them
That is the second lesson: even those who rightly judge and discipline a person for committing a particular sin are not necessarily protected from committing it themselves.
Taking a right and necessary action is not the same as taking sufficient action.
The truth is, there is only one kind of leader in this world, and that’s a flawed leader.
The wise among these flawed leaders are the ones who are most aware of their flaws and who actively seek them out, take action against them, and invite others to do the same.
